en: The *Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Kingdom of Sālā*, translated by an unknown person and now appended to the Eastern Jin Record.
Formerly there was a great kingdom named Sālā; its territory was vast and expansive, and in its center lay a place of solemn purity.

The population was vast, prosperous, and flourishing; the people were skillful, clever, elegant, and fond of elaborate adornments. It produced many precious treasures in five colors—black, yellow, red, white, and blue.

The city walls, towers, pavilions, streets, alleys, gates, and chambers were coated with gold and silver, square and round, pure and beautiful. Around the city, lotuses grew in bathing pools where ducks, geese, mandarin ducks, pigeons, *lao* birds, peacocks, parrots, *yan-sui* birds, cormorants, and *fan-fei* birds flew about in pursuit of one another; they all dwelt within the pools, resting day and night and warbling harmoniously together.

Men and women engaged in play, performing as courtesans and musicians; they never grew weary, and their pleasure was beyond description. Clinging to self-indulgence and arrogance, they did not understand the Buddha-dharma, each finding such personal satisfaction that they considered themselves peerless in the world.
The Buddha was staying at the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī.

Seeing that the people of this country were so engrossed in worldly pleasures and failed to contemplate the suffering of impermanence and the cycle of birth and death, greedily indulging in impure sensual desires without any sense of weariness, [the Buddha reflected].
The Buddha reflected that birth and death were flourishing in that land and that because its inhabitants did not practice skillful wisdom, who could deliver them?
He immediately employed expedient means to transform their minds, saying:

"All forms and appearances should be met with emptiness; all pleasures and joys should be met with suffering. Through the exercise of skillful means according to their inclinations, they shall be led to detach from conceptualization and consciousness."

The Buddha then manifested the divine *ṛddhi-samādhi*, emitting a great radiance that shone everywhere, moving the eight directions as well as humans and non-humans; the devas, nāgas, and spirits followed and attended him from behind.

Śakra and Brahmā held precious canopies made of the seven jewels and offered them to serve the Buddha. Maitreya, Mañjuśrī, Maudgalyāyana, Rāhula, Ānanda, Revata, Śāriputra, and thousands of other disciples and bodhisattvas all followed and accompanied him.

In that land, the hundred birds, beasts, and domestic animals cried out in harmony with one another; the various musical instruments of the performers resounded spontaneously without being struck. Withered trees and all vegetation grew anew of their own accord. Among the turtles, tortoises, *yuan*, and *ge*—all species belonging to the watery realm in the ditches, channels, rivers, and seas—there was none that did not rejoice. The three thousandfold world-system shook violently; lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels sprang from the earth, composed of a mingling of rare jewels and lapis lazuli, their exquisite colors dazzling the eyes of men.
The Buddha emitted a radiance that shone everywhere; all those places of profound darkness and diligent suffering were completely opened up and became free of any obstruction.
Kings, ministers, elders, householders, palace princes, noble ladies, and beauties—among the citizens, both great and small—were all struck with awe, wondering:
"For what reason today has such a manifestation appeared?"
"Within the palace of the Lord of Freedom, one may amuse oneself with the five kinds of music; the joy of courtesans beating drums cannot surpass this. What we have seen now is rare in the world.
At that time, the Earth-holding Deity leaped forth from the ground and appeared before the king's palace, praising the Buddha’s merits:

"The World-Honored One manifests transformations whose radiance exceeds that of the sun and moon; all devas look up to him in reverence, and he is honored by Śakra and Brahmā. Having already removed the defilements of the world, he liberates humanity from birth and death."

Those who behold the Buddha have their transgressions and sins eliminated; those who make offerings to the Buddha receive immeasurable doublefold merit. By planting the roots of virtue, one will be reborn in the heavens in a future life; the infinite rewards gained from giving rise to a single thought of wisdom are boundless. You should go to see the Buddha and inquire about and receive his words of Dharma.
The king’s mind subsequently opened and he rejoiced within himself, thinking:
“The Tathāgata has descended as a spirit within my realm, and all sentient beings are being delivered.
Not only he himself, but his entire retinue and the rest of the multitude all went out of the city, filled with joy and leaping for gladness.
Through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, this realm was made vast and brilliantly illuminated, penetrating boundlessly.
The king and his people all went to see the Buddha, exclaiming, "How wonderful!"
The roots of merit give rise to wholesome thoughts!

Beholding the Buddha’s venerable countenance, its golden light shines resplendently; his majestic power surges forth as he is adorned with auspiciousness; his marks are bright and clear, and his mind is tranquil and serene.

The king and the people all stepped forward to pay homage to the Buddha; bowing their heads to the ground in prostration, they circumambulated the Honored One three times and then stood before him to recount their circumstances:
"For a long time we have been submerged in greed and turbidity, deluded by sounds and forms, and thus failed to see the Tathāgata to serve him and inquire about the Dharma."
The Buddha said,
"Excellent! Are the King,
his ministers and subjects, and the members of the inner court and the crown prince all in peace?"
The King said,
"Having received the Buddha's grace, all is as it should be.
The Buddha said:

“The King is greedy for sensual pleasures and indulges his heart without satiety; he levies taxes to amass wealth and treasures, prepares delicacies of manifold flavors, and finds endless delight in gardens, pavilions, and bathing pools. Failing to contemplate impermanence, what benefit could there be in these things even in the slightest degree?”

When humans are bound by desire, it does not only affect their future lives; they are immediately cast into the realms of hell and animals. Merely because of insatiable craving, they are scorched and roasted until their bodies are mangled; starving, they cannot find food, and parched, they have no water to drink. In constant terror and bitter anguish, they torment one another—all this results from a lack of foresight, rebellious hearts, and the commission of evil.

"Though one possesses wealth and a position of high honor within the deep palace during one's lifetime, all of this is impermanent, like awakening from a dream; I imagine that when my life ends, I shall be born alone, with not a single person to follow me.
The King knelt before him and addressed the World-Honored One:
"World-Honored One!"
"By what skillful means may we be freed from this transgression?

The Buddha is the Dharma King to whom all turn for refuge; the Buddha is the Right Honored One whom all sentient beings revere and look up to. We pray that you will lift us up so that we may escape this suffering."
The Buddha said: “Excellent!
O King, establish the foundation of faith and practice the four deeds; thus you may be freed from transgression.”
First, to give all that one possesses without any sense of attachment or stinginess;
second, to have few desires and no anger, and to sever and diminish greed for food;
third, to hear the Buddha’s sutras and precepts, to believe and accept them, and not to transgress them.
The fourth is to revere and be cautious toward Dharma masters and to cherish spiritual friends.
These are the four matters by which one may attain purity.
The King, conceiving a thought of wishing to offer great almsgiving, stepped forward, prostrated before the Honored One, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that you would deign to visit my palace for a modest meal.
The Buddha remained silent, thereby accepting the invitation.
The King returned to his palace and commanded his ministers and officials:
"A Buddha is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower; now that we have encountered one, we should offer him proper worship.

We shall bring forth various flowers, incense, banners, streamers, and music; we shall adorn the palace chambers and sweep them clean, and throughout the streets and alleys of the city, we shall provide banners and canopies."

The Queen of the Inner Palace and all the people of the kingdom received the King’s instructions; they prepared the seats and immediately commanded the Chief Cook to prepare food of a hundred flavors, seasoned with fragrant sweetness. Then they went out to welcome the Buddha, saying:
"The offerings are ready; we pray that you will deign to accept our service."

The Buddha, at that very moment, attained [realization] while seated; he then manifested his majestic spiritual power, moving the entire assembly. The fourfold disciples, hundreds of thousands of devas and humans, as well as the nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and others, surrounded him with their retinues and followed the Buddha. With the Four Heavenly Kings leading the way and Śakra and Brahmā holding a parasol, the bodhisattva mahāsattvas attended the Buddha as he entered the city.

When the Buddha stepped upon the threshold of the gate, the entire realm shook; those who were blind, deaf, mute, afflicted by poison, disease, or emaciation were all restored to their former wholeness and health, and lutes and musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck.

The Buddha emitted a radiance that illuminated all the palaces; the city walls, houses, and dwellings were all transformed into lapis lazuli, so transparent inside and out that everyone could see the Buddha.

The Buddha ascended the hall before him and took his place upon the lion throne. The king, the crown prince, the state ministers, and the common people immediately set forth the food and drink, serving it with their own hands. When the meal was finished, they offered water for washing the mouth and hands, and all the people took their seats.

The king took a small stool and sat before him to listen to the sutra; as the Buddha turned the wheel of Dharma and preached on non-retrogression, the king was filled with joy and offered his robe to the Buddha—a garment worth ten million pieces of gold, a rarity in the world.

The robes that were scattered hung suspended in the void, whereupon they transformed above the Buddha into a jeweled canopy. From this canopy, seven precious gems formed an interlaced lattice, all of which hung with pearls.
From these hanging pearls issued forth radiance, which shone everywhere throughout the countless Buddha-lands of the ten directions.

The king, his ministers and subjects, the women of the inner palace, the crown prince, the consorts, and beautiful maidens—altogether more than ten thousand people—beheld these transformations and were all moved with exultation. They all conceived the aspiration for unexcelled, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). Eight hundred celestial deities attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma-kṣānti*), five thousand bodhisattvas established themselves in the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*), and countless thousands of people cultivated the roots of virtue; after their lives ended, they were all reborn in the heavens.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This king has served more than five hundred Buddhas, practicing generosity with wealth and treasures while exercising compassion; he has honored the Dharma without weariness. In a future kalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood, known by the name Tathāgata Prabhāsa, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The people of this kingdom and all the ladies shall likewise receive his merit and all shall attain Buddhahood."
Upon hearing this prophecy, the king leaped into the air, manifesting his body at a height of one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground. Descending from above, he praised the Buddha’s merits:
“The Buddha is most venerable, serving as the foundation for all beings; his virtue is like the heavens, covering all without exception!”
When the eight thousand people of the country heard that the King had received the prophecy, they all gave rise to pure minds and vowed to become bodhisattvas.
When the Buddha finished preaching this sutra, the entire assembly, including humans and non-humans, was filled with joy.
Such is the transformation effected by the World-Honored One’s skillful means.
*The Sutra on the Kingdom of Sala Spoken by the Buddha*.
